newsitem.title: USA: Colombia hails 1st-ever $1.0 bln global bond deal.
newsitem.headline: Colombia hails 1st-ever $1.0 bln global bond deal.

text.p: Colombia's $1.0 billion first-ever global bond deal achieved its objectives in reaching full global distribution and excellent pricing, said Clemente del Valle, director general of Public Credit for Colombia.

"From the price point of view, it was an excellent priced deal for us. It was our first global and we achieved all the objectives of what we had aimed to do which was to get a real global distribution," Clemente del Valle told Reuters in a telephone interview.
He said distribution on the 10-year tranche consisted of 64 percent in the U.S., 16 percent in Europe, 18 percent in Asia, and two percent in Latin America.
As for the 30-year tranche of Colombia's global, Del Valle said the breakdown was 53 percent in the U.S., 29 percent in Europe, 14 percent in Asia and four percent in Latin America.
Del Valle said he believed non-U.S. participation on the 30-year was a record in terms of its broad distribution.

He said the maturities on the global bond meet Colombia's yield curve objectives. "I think it is worth mentioning that in the dollar market we have accomplished probably the most complete yield curve by any emerging market sovereign in this market. Now we have a very full three to 30-year yield curve with strong benchmarks all around the yield curve."

Colombia's 10-year tranche totalled $750 million and was priced at 99.707 to yield 130 basis points over comparable U.S. Treasuries. The 30-year portion was $250 million priced at 99.884 to yield 170 basis points over U.S. Treasuries.

The global bond offering was issued via joint lead managers J.P. Morgan Securities and Merrill Lynch & Co. The issue is rated Baa-3 by Moody's Investors Service and BBB-minus by Standard & Poor's Corp.

In terms of future borrowings, del Valle said Colombia had met most of its funding needs for the first semester but it would issue another $400 to $500 million later this year in German marks and yen.

"With this deal we have funded most of the first semester needs so that is quite an achievement for us. We still have $400 to $500 million remaining to be funded. We will probably try to give some preference to the Asian and European segments in the yen and deutschemark where we want to keep a presence," said del Valle.
Proceeds from Colombia's global bond issue will be used for general budgetary purposes, del Valle said.
